summary: Learners build the atom 	a2192 element 	a2192 compound 	a2192 mixture hierarchy by assembling atoms rather than memorising definitions. The core conceptual moves: an element is one kind of atom; a compound is two or more kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio and has NEW properties unlike its elements; a mixture is substances together but physically separable. Learners also read simple formulae as 'how many of each atom', match chemical symbols, and meet a light introduction to atomic structure: a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons in shells around it. Detailed electron-shell arrangement is kept light at this stage.
misconceptions: A compound is just a mixture of its elements and keeps their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by physical means (filtering, etc.).
The subscript in a formula multiplies the whole formula rather than the preceding atom.
Elements and atoms are the same thing (confusing the substance with its building block).
A molecule of an element (e.g. O2) must be a compound because it has two atoms.

activities.title: Atom workshop: build and classify
steps: Drag atoms from a palette and snap identical atoms together (e.g. two blue atoms) 	a2014 observe the classifier label the result 'element'.
Snap different atoms together (e.g. two blue + one red) and watch a formula box write the compound's formula while the classifier flips to 'compound'.

Scatter a jumble of two or more DIFFERENT kinds of separate particles that are not joined to each other (e.g. some blue–blue molecules alongside some separate red atoms) and observe the classifier read 'mixture'; note that a jumble of identical molecules is still one pure substance, not a mixture.
Use a 'try to separate' tool: pull a mixture cleanly into its parts, then try the same on a compound and find it cannot be pulled apart physically.
State in your own words why the built thing is an element, a compound, or a mixture, and read the formula off your model as a count of each kind of atom.
activities.insight: Element, compound and mixture are distinguished by how atoms are arranged: one kind of atom (element), different kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio (compound), or substances merely together and separable (mixture). A formula records how many of each atom are joined.

activities.title: New properties: a compound is not its elements
steps: Compare the properties of reactive sodium metal and poisonous chlorine gas, then observe (via demonstration or described reaction) that combined they form ordinary edible table salt (NaCl).
State what changed: the compound has its OWN properties, different from both elements.
Predict for iron filings mixed with sulfur powder: can a magnet still pull out the iron, and does it still look like iron + sulfur? (Yes 	a2014 it is a mixture; each part keeps its own properties.)

Then consider a fresh portion heated to form dark grey iron sulfide and predict whether the magnet still pulls out iron (No, if all the iron has reacted: a new compound has formed. In real demonstrations leftover unreacted iron may still be attracted, so any pull comes from leftover iron, not from the compound).
Explain the difference between the two iron/sulfur results in terms of 'just together' versus 'chemically joined'.
activities.insight: When elements chemically combine into a compound, the compound has genuinely new properties, unlike a mixture where each component keeps its own properties and can be separated physically.

activities.title: Atom structure and symbol reference
steps: Explore a labelled atom diagram showing a tiny central nucleus 	a2014 containing protons and neutrons 	a2014 with electrons arranged around it in shells, together with the element's chemical symbol (the electron-shell detail is kept light at this stage).
Match chemical symbols to their elements using a symbol key.

Read given formulae (e.g. H2O, CO2, NaCl) aloud, naming each element and how many atoms of each are present (for NaCl, which is not made of separate molecules, read the formula as a 1:1 ratio of sodium to chlorine).
Decide for each example whether it is an element or a compound and justify it.
activities.insight: Atoms have internal structure 	a2014 a central nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it 	a2014 and chemical symbols are a shorthand; a formula names the elements present and the number of atoms of each. Detailed electron arrangement is kept light at this stage.

activities.title: Classify and build: check understanding
steps: Classify given particle diagrams as element, compound or mixture and justify each choice.
Match chemical symbols to their elements.
Build or complete a formula by filling in how many of each atom for a described molecule.
Transfer to fresh cases: water, carbon dioxide (CO2), sodium chloride (NaCl), and iron sulfide.
activities.insight: Learners can apply the element/compound/mixture distinction, read and write simple formulae, and transfer the 'new properties / not physically separable' idea to new substances.

checkQuestion: Water has the formula H₂O — it's made from hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen burns and oxygen is the gas fires need. So would you expect water to burn, or to help things burn? Then the important part: explain why water behaves the way it does, given what it's made of.
checkAnswer: No — water does neither; it puts fires out. When elements combine into a COMPOUND, the compound has completely NEW properties, not the properties of the elements it came from. Hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in water and no longer behave as the separate elements. Full marks need 'a compound's properties are new, unlike a mixture where each part keeps its own'.
